levels.title: Market Literacy
levels.intro: This level covers the arithmetic used in markets: percentages, basis points, powers, logarithms, compounding, discounting, annuities and returns. It describes stocks, bonds and funds, the main market participants, and how a trade moves from order to custody. It also covers client-account setup, double-entry posting of a trade, and the average, variance and normal curve.

modules.title: Algebra & Functions Refresh
modules.hook: Percentages, basis points, powers, logarithms and simple equations as used in fee, return and doubling-time calculations. Short drills with hints and unlimited retries.

units.title: Percentages, basis points and proportions
objectives: Learner can convert between percent, decimal and basis points
Learner can compute a percentage change and chain successive percentage changes
Learner can compute a fee or a weight as a percentage of an amount
key_concepts: weights and shares of a total
units.worked_example: A EUR 25,000 portfolio pays a 0.45% (45 bp) annual custody fee = EUR 112.50. A fund that falls 20% and then rises 25% is exactly back at its start, because 0.80 x 1.25 = 1.00; falling 20% and rising 20% leaves it 4% short.

exercises.task: Warm-up check (no score pressure): pick the correct decimal and bp equivalent of a stated percentage
exercises.params: percentage drawn from 0.05%-3.5%; distractors are off-by-10 and off-by-100 errors

exercises.task: Compute the annual fee in EUR from a portfolio value and a fee in bp
exercises.params: value EUR 5,000-2,000,000; fee 5-150 bp; step hints show bp -> decimal -> multiply

exercises.task: Find the percentage change between two prices, then the price after a stated percentage move
exercises.params: start price EUR 5-500; move -35% to +60%; tolerance 0.01

exercises.task: Chain two or three successive percentage moves into one total move
exercises.params: moves between -30% and +40%; asks for total % change to 2 decimals

exercises.task: Pair headline statements with their correct reading (percent vs percentage points, e.g. yield rises from 2.0% to 2.5%)
exercises.params: 4-5 pairs from a bank of 20 rate/yield/fee headlines

exercises.task: Fill in the blanks of a short fee statement with amounts, bp and percentages
exercises.params: random fee schedule; word bank with one distractor

units.worked_example: How many whole shares can EUR 10,000 buy at EUR 37.60 if there is a flat EUR 9.90 fee? Solve n x 37.60 + 9.90 <= 10,000, so n = 265 shares (cost EUR 9,964.00 + 9.90 = EUR 9,973.90).

exercises.task: Solve for quantity, price or amount in 'amount = quantity x price' with a hidden unknown
exercises.params: which variable is hidden is randomised; values with 2-3 decimals

Learner can convert a multi-year growth factor into a per-year factor using roots
Learner can read and write large amounts in millions, billions and scientific notation
units.worked_example: EUR 1 grows to EUR 1.21 in 2 years, so the yearly factor is 1.21^(1/2) = 1.10, i.e. 10% a year. A company with 3.2 x 10^9 shares at EUR 45 has a market capitalisation of EUR 144 bn.

exercises.params: fee rule with min fee EUR 3-15, rate 0.05%-0.25%, optional cap

units.title: Exponential functions and growth
objectives: Learner can evaluate f(t) = a x b^t for growth and decay
Learner can tell linear from exponential growth from a table or a graph
Learner can state what the number e is for and evaluate e^x
units.worked_example: EUR 1,000 growing at 4% a year is worth 1,000 x 1.04^10 = EUR 1,480.24 after 10 years, versus EUR 1,400 if only the original EUR 1,000 earned 4% each year. Rule of 72: 72/4 = 18 years to double, close to the exact 17.7.

exercises.task: Compute the value after t years of growth at a given yearly rate
Sort sequences or tables into 'linear' or 'exponential'
exercises.params: 8 generated data series with random start and step/factor

units.title: Logarithms
objectives: Learner can use a logarithm as the inverse of an exponential to solve for time or rate
Learner can apply the product, quotient and power rules
Learner can read a log-scale chart and explain why log charts show percentage moves
key_concepts: log scale and constant percentage change
units.worked_example: How long to double at 4% a year? Solve 1.04^t = 2, so t = ln 2 / ln 1.04 = 0.6931 / 0.03922 = 17.67 years. On a log chart a 10% rise looks the same size at EUR 10 and at EUR 100.

Learner can recognise which kind of sequence a data series follows
Learner can find a missing term or the common difference/ratio
units.worked_example: A savings plan starts at EUR 100 a month and rises by EUR 10 each month: the 12th instalment is 100 + 11 x 10 = EUR 210 (arithmetic). A dividend of EUR 2.00 growing 5% a year pays 2.00 x 1.05^4 = EUR 2.43 in year 5 (geometric).

units.title: Series, sigma notation and a mixed drill round
objectives: Learner can read and expand sigma notation
Learner can sum a finite geometric series with the formula and the infinite series when the ratio is below 1
Learner can combine percentages, powers, logs and series in a mixed set
key_concepts: finite geometric sum S = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)
units.worked_example: Sum of 1.05^-k for k = 1..5 is (1 - 1.05^-5)/0.05 = 4.3295; this is exactly the present value of EUR 1 a year for 5 years at 5%, which F1 will name an annuity factor. The infinite version gives 1/0.05 = 20.

exercises.task: Evaluate a sigma expression by expansion
exercises.params: k from 1 to 3-8; term = linear or power of k

exercises.task: Sum the first n terms of a geometric series with the closed formula

exercises.params: error from {wrong n, wrong first term, ignored r > 1}

units.title: Simple interest and the time value of money
objectives: Learner can compute simple interest over a fractional period with an Act/360 style day count
Learner can explain why money today beats money later
Learner can distinguish nominal rate, period and amount
key_concepts: simple interest I = P x r x t
day count basics (Act/360, Act/365) as a preview
money-market quoting (EURIBOR, EUR short rate as reference examples)
units.worked_example: EUR 500,000 lent for 90 days at 3.20% on Act/360: interest = 500,000 x 0.032 x 90/360 = EUR 4,000. With Act/365 the same loan pays EUR 3,945.21, which is why conventions matter.

units.title: Compounding and future value
objectives: Learner can compute future value with annual and sub-annual compounding
Learner can compute the effective annual rate (EAR) from a nominal rate and compounding frequency
Learner can compute continuously compounded growth and use it to compare rates
units.worked_example: EUR 20,000 for 10 years at 3% compounded annually becomes 20,000 x 1.03^10 = EUR 26,878.33. A 3% nominal rate compounded monthly gives EAR = (1 + 0.03/12)^12 - 1 = 3.042%; continuous compounding gives e^0.03 - 1 = 3.045%.

exercises.task: Compute the future value of a lump sum with annual compounding

Learner can compute the present value of several cash flows and compare options
Learner can solve for the discount rate or the number of periods
key_concepts: present value of a cash-flow list
solving for r or n with roots and logs
units.worked_example: A zero-coupon note repays EUR 1,000 in 5 years; at a 4% discount rate it is worth 1,000 / 1.04^5 = EUR 821.93. If it trades at EUR 800, the yield satisfies (1,000/800)^(1/5) - 1 = 4.56%.

units.title: Returns: holding-period, annualised, real and nominal

units.worked_example: A share bought at EUR 40, paying a EUR 1.20 dividend and sold at EUR 43 after 18 months, has HPR (43 - 40 + 1.20)/40 = 10.5%, or 6.9% a year geometrically. With 2.5% inflation, the real return is 1.069/1.025 - 1 = 4.3% a year.

Average cost = (10,000 + 6,120)/800 = 20.15; realised on 600 = 600 x 0.55 = 330; unrealised on 200 = 200 x 0.45 = 90; total 420. units.title: Vectors and portfolio weights
objectives: Learner can add vectors and multiply a vector by a scalar, including a leverage scale-up

units.worked_example: Weights (0.5, 0.3, 0.2) and expected returns (6%, 4%, 10%): w . r = 0.03 + 0.012 + 0.02 = 6.2%. From EUR holdings (250k, 150k, 100k) the weights are holdings / 500k = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2). Scaling the weights by 1.5 gives (0.75, 0.45, 0.30), a 150% gross exposure financed by a 50% loan, and return 1.5 x 6.2% = 9.3% before interest.

exercises.task: Dot product of weights and returns
Weights from EUR holdings

Which operation is valid?

units.title: Matrices and operations
objectives: Learner can multiply two 2x2 matrices and a 2x2 matrix by a 2x1 vector
Learner can state when a product is defined from the dimensions
Learner can transpose a vector or matrix and recognise a symmetric matrix
Learner can use the identity matrix
key_concepts: dimension rule (m x n)(n x p)
units.worked_example: [[1,2],[3,4]] x [[0,1],[1,0]] = [[2,1],[4,3]] (multiplying by a swap matrix swaps columns). Covariance matrix [[0.04, 0.006],[0.006, 0.01]] times weights (0.5, 0.5) gives (0.023, 0.008), the first step of portfolio variance. A 2x1 times 2x1 product is undefined: the shapes do not match.

exercises.task: Entry of a 2x2 product
Matrix-vector product
Is the product defined, and what shape?
Complete a transposed matrix
Which matrix is symmetric?

units.title: Linear systems and inverses
objectives: Learner can solve a 2x2 system by elimination and by the inverse

exercises.task: Solution of a 2x2 system

Is the matrix invertible?
Inverse entry

units.title: Covariance matrices
objectives: Learner can compute a covariance from volatilities and correlation, and the reverse
Learner can compute a sample covariance from a short return series
Learner can build a 2x2 and 3x3 covariance matrix
Learner can recognise an invalid covariance matrix (correlation outside [-1,1], negative variance)
units.worked_example: Volatilities 20% and 10% with correlation 0.3: covariance 0.3 x 0.2 x 0.1 = 0.006; matrix [[0.04, 0.006],[0.006, 0.01]]. From returns X = (2, -1, 3, 0)% and Y = (1, 0, 2, 1)%: means 1 and 1, products of deviations (0, 2, 2, 0) sum 4, sample covariance 4 / 3 = 1.33 %^2. The matrix [[0.04, 0.05],[0.05, 0.01]] implies correlation 2.5, so it is invalid.

exercises.task: Covariance from volatilities and correlation
Correlation from a covariance matrix
Sample covariance from a return series
Build the covariance matrix
Is the matrix a valid covariance matrix?

units.title: Portfolio variance as w'Σw
objectives: Learner can compute portfolio variance as w'Sigma w for 2 and 3 assets
Learner can compute the minimum-variance weights for two assets
Learner can compare portfolio volatility with the weighted average volatility
Learner can explain diversification as a consequence of correlation below 1
key_concepts: min-variance weight w1 = (s2^2 - s12)/(s1^2 + s2^2 - 2 s12)
units.worked_example: With the Q6.4 assets at 50/50: variance = 0.25 x 0.04 + 0.25 x 0.01 + 2 x 0.25 x 0.006 = 0.0155, volatility 12.45%, against a weighted average of 15%. Minimum variance: w1 = (0.01 - 0.006)/(0.04 + 0.01 - 0.012) = 10.5% in the 20%-vol asset, 89.5% in the other, variance 0.00958 (vol 9.79%), below either asset alone.

exercises.task: Portfolio variance for two assets
Min-variance weight
Portfolio volatility vs weighted average
Does diversification reduce risk?
Variance when correlation is 1 or -1

units.title: Eigenvalues and principal components
objectives: Learner can find the eigenvalues of a 2x2 covariance matrix from trace and determinant
Learner can find the direction (eigenvector) of the largest eigenvalue
Learner can compute the share of variance explained by each component
Learner can interpret PCA factors of a yield curve (level, slope, curvature)
units.worked_example: For [[0.04, 0.006],[0.006, 0.01]]: trace 0.05, determinant 0.000364, eigenvalues (0.05 +/- sqrt(0.0025 - 0.001456))/2 = 0.04116 and 0.00884. The first component explains 0.04116 / 0.05 = 82.3% of variance with direction about (0.98, 0.19), mostly the 20%-vol asset. In yield-curve PCA the first three components typically explain the vast majority of variation (level, slope, curvature).

exercises.task: Eigenvalues of a 2x2 matrix

units.title: Consolidation: risk of a Lombard pool
objectives: Learner can build a 3x3 covariance matrix and compute pool volatility with w'Sigma w

units.worked_example: Pool EUR 1m: equities 40% (vol 20%), equity fund 20% (15%), IG bonds 40% (5%), correlations 0.8, 0.1, 0.2. Variance = 0.0121, vol 11.0%, below the 13% weighted average. 1-day 99% loss = 11.0% / sqrt(252) x 2.326 x 1m = EUR 16.1k (undiversified: EUR 19.1k); 10-day 51k. Haircuts of 50%, 40%, 30% give a EUR 400k cushion, far above VaR because they cover stressed gaps and a 20-day liquidation.

1-day 99% loss in EUR

exercises.task: Compute mean and sd of an n-step walk
Rescale a daily vol to annual and vice versa
Doubling the horizon multiplies the sd by what?

units.title: Brownian motion: definition and properties

Compute probabilities of events about W(t) using increments and the normal distribution
Explain why paths are continuous but nowhere differentiable, in words

exercises.task: Probability that W(t) exceeds a level
Covariance and correlation of W(s) and W(t)

Distribution of X(t) = mu t + sigma W(t) at a horizon

units.title: Quadratic variation: why ordinary calculus fails
objectives: Compute the quadratic variation of a Brownian path and of a smooth path
Use the rule (dW)^2 = dt, dt dW = 0, (dt)^2 = 0 mechanically
Explain in a sentence why this produces the extra term in Itô's formula
units.worked_example: Daily log returns with sd 1.26% across 252 days give realised QV 252 x 0.0126^2 = 0.040, i.e. annualised vol 20%: the sum of squares converges, the sum of absolute values grows with finer sampling.

exercises.task: Realised variance and vol from a series of 10 returns
Which process has non-zero quadratic variation?

units.title: The Itô integral: building stochastic integrals
objectives: Describe the Itô integral as the limit of sums with left-endpoint evaluation
State mean-zero and Itô isometry and compute variance of simple integrals
Explain in words why the integral of W dW is (W^2 - t)/2 and not W^2/2
units.worked_example: The integral of W dW from 0 to T: the extra -T/2 is exactly the quadratic-variation correction; E[integral] = 0 consistent with E[W^2 - T] = 0.

exercises.task: Compute variance of the integral of c dW or of t dW with Itô isometry
Why must the integrand be evaluated at the left endpoint?

units.title: Itô's lemma: the chain rule for diffusions
objectives: Apply Itô's lemma to functions of W and of t and W
Derive the SDE of S^2, ln S and 1/S given dS = mu S dt + sigma S dW
Explain the -sigma^2/2 correction in the log

units.worked_example: For f = ln S: d ln S = (mu - sigma^2/2)dt + sigma dW; with mu = 8% and sigma = 20% the median grows at 6%, not 8%.

exercises.task: Compute the drift of ln S, S^2 or sqrt(S) from mu and sigma
Order the mechanical steps of an Itô computation
Tabulate f_t, f_x, f_xx then assemble drift and diffusion for f(S)
Spot the error in a derivation that uses ordinary chain rule
Why is the median of S(T) below its mean?

units.title: Geometric Brownian motion and solving SDEs
objectives: Solve the GBM SDE explicitly and read off moments and quantiles of S(T)
Simulate (conceptually) a path with the exact log-step
Compare arithmetic and geometric returns in a continuous-time setting
key_concepts: lognormal moments E[S] = S0 e^{mu T}
units.worked_example: S0 = 100, mu = 8%, sigma = 20%, T = 5: E[S] = 149.2, median = 100 e^{0.06x5} = 134.9, 5% quantile of the log-return distribution via z = -1.645.

exercises.task: Mean, median and 95% interval of S(T)
Probability the stock ends above a threshold at T
Volatility drag: difference between arithmetic and geometric average growth
Which discretisation preserves positivity of S?

units.title: Mean reversion and other SDEs: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck, CIR, Vasicek
objectives: Write and interpret OU / Vasicek / CIR dynamics and their long-run behaviour
Compute conditional mean and variance for an OU process
Link the PDE (Feynman-Kac) and expectation views conceptually
key_concepts: short-rate models as inputs for F4
units.worked_example: Vasicek with a = 0.5, b = 3%, sigma = 1%: after 2 years the expected rate from r0 = 1% is 3% - 2% e^{-1} = 2.26%, and the stationary sd is 1%/sqrt(1) = 1%.

exercises.task: Conditional mean at horizon t for OU/Vasicek
Stationary variance sigma^2 / 2a
Match models to features: GBM, OU, CIR, jump-diffusion
Sort quantities into 'can go negative' vs 'cannot'

units.title: Girsanov, risk-neutral measure and the martingale representation
objectives: State what changing measure does to drift and not to volatility
Derive the risk-neutral dynamics of a stock from the real-world ones
Explain the roles of Girsanov and martingale representation in completeness of Black-Scholes
key_concepts: market price of risk theta = (mu - r)/sigma
units.worked_example: mu = 9%, r = 2%, sigma = 20%: theta = 0.35; under Q the stock drifts at r; same volatility, so vol is observable while mu is not needed for pricing.

exercises.task: Market price of risk and Sharpe ratio from mu, r, sigma

modules.title: Asset pricing theory
modules.hook: Stochastic discount factors, the consumption-based first-order condition, and the derivation of the CAPM and factor models from it.

units.title: Preferences, utility and risk aversion
objectives: Compute expected utility and certainty equivalent for a lottery under CRRA and CARA
Derive absolute and relative risk aversion for given utility functions
Link risk aversion to the required premium for a risky asset
units.worked_example: Log utility, 50/50 gamble on wealth 80 or 120 EUR: EU = 0.5 ln 80 + 0.5 ln 120 = 4.5847, certainty equivalent 97.98 < 100, risk premium about 2.0 EUR.

exercises.task: Certainty equivalent of a gamble under power utility
Relative risk aversion from derivatives u', u'' (calculus drill)
Which preference ranking holds as gamma rises?
Match utility functions to CRRA/CARA/neither

units.title: The fundamental equation: stochastic discount factor
objectives: Derive price = E[m x] from a two-period investor problem
Use the SDF to price a bond, a stock and a zero-cost excess return
Decompose the risk premium into -cov(m, R)
units.worked_example: m takes 1.1 in a bad state (p = 0.4) and 0.7 in a good state (p = 0.6); E[m] = 0.86 so Rf = 16.3%; a payoff paying 100 in the bad state only is worth 44 EUR.

exercises.task: Price a payoff given state probabilities and SDF values
Risk premium from cov(m, R)
Sequence the steps of the derivation from investor FOC to price
Why is an asset positively correlated with consumption growth risky?
Complete a state-price table: probability, m, payoff, contribution

objectives: Show that any beta-pricing model corresponds to an SDF linear in factors
Use the Hansen-Jagannathan bound to bound the SDF volatility from Sharpe ratios
Compare CAPM and mean-variance frontiers in SDF language
units.worked_example: Equity Sharpe ratio 0.4: sigma(m)/E(m) must be at least 0.4. With CRRA = 2 and consumption growth vol 1.5%, sigma(m) is only about 3%, a large gap.

exercises.task: Minimum SDF volatility implied by a Sharpe ratio
Convert a CAPM beta and market premium into an SDF coefficient b

Match each model (CAPM, CCAPM, APT) to its SDF form

units.title: Consumption-based asset pricing and the equity premium puzzle
objectives: Compute equity premium implied by CRRA preferences and consumption growth
State the Mehra-Prescott puzzle and the risk-free rate puzzle
List the main directions out of the puzzles
units.worked_example: Historical premium 6%, consumption-growth vol 1.5%, correlation with stock 0.2, stock vol 16%: gamma = 6% / (0.2 x 1.5% x 16%) = 125, implausibly high.

exercises.task: Compute implied gamma from premium and covariance

Explain why habit makes marginal utility counter-cyclical and raises risk premia
Evaluate the empirical realism of each approach

exercises.task: Match each mechanism to the puzzle it targets

Surplus consumption ratio dynamics, one-step update

Interpret GMM moment conditions E[m R^e] = 0 and pricing-error tests

convergence of Riemann sums vs Itô sums

exercises.task: E[X | partition cell] on a finite space

Conditional expectation minimises which loss?

units.title: Monte Carlo: the idea, its error and its limits

units.title: Variance reduction, Greeks by simulation and American options
